terms.title: Albedo
terms.summary: Albedo is essentially another word for Base color. Base Color/Albedo is a map without lighting, shadow, or highlights.

terms.title: Base Color
terms.summary: Basecolor is essentially another word for Albedo. Base Color/Albedo is a map without lighting, shadow, or highlights.

terms.title: Roughness
terms.summary:
A roughness map controls how light scatters across a material's surface, determining whether reflections appear sharp and glossy or soft and diffuse. In a PBR workflow, roughness is often the most important map for creating realism because it defines a material's surface quality and wear. Variations in roughness can represent scratches, fingerprints, dirt, polished areas, worn edges, and other subtle details that make materials feel believable. Even when two objects share the same Base Color, different roughness values can make them appear completely different under lighting.

Key takeaway: A realistic Roughness map usually contains meaningful variation rather than a single uniform value. Surface response often contributes more to realism than additional color detail.

terms.title: Beveling
terms.summary: Beveling (also called chamfering) is the process of rounding or flattening the edge of a 3D model. This helps surfaces catch highlights, improves realism, and is critical for producing clean high-poly models for baking.

terms.title: ZBrush
terms.summary: ZBrush is a digital sculpting application used to create highly detailed models. Artists can work with millions of polygons, making it ideal for organic forms, characters, and high-resolution detail work in games and film.

terms.title: Smooth Mesh Preview
terms.summary: Smooth Mesh Preview in Maya allows artists to preview a subdivided (smoothed) version of their model without permanently applying subdivision. It is used to visualize how a low-poly cage will look when smoothed.

terms.title: Dynamesh
terms.summary: Dynamesh is a ZBrush feature that redistributes topology evenly across a mesh while sculpting. It behaves like a voxel-based system, allowing shapes to merge and change freely without stretched polygons, but does not maintain clean, animation-ready topology.

terms.title: Remeshing
terms.summary: Remeshing regenerates the topology of a mesh, but behaves very differently depending on the software. In ZBrush, Remesh tools (like ZRemesher) produce clean, all-quad topology with even edge flow ideal for sculpting. In Maya, the Remesh tool behaves more like a voxelizer, producing a triangulated mesh similar to Dynamesh, which is NOT ideal for sculpting or animation. Because of this, Maya users typically use the Retopologize tool instead when they need clean, quad-based topology.

terms.title: Retopology
terms.summary: Retopology is the process of rebuilding a mesh with clean, efficient topology. In Maya, the Retopologize tool is used to create evenly distributed, quad-based geometry suitable for animation and production. Unlike Maya’s Remesh (which creates triangulated, voxel-like output), Retopologize produces structured edge flow similar to ZBrush’s ZRemesher, making it the preferred tool for creating production-ready meshes.

terms.title: 12 Principles of Animation
terms.summary: The 12 Principles of Animation are foundational guidelines created by Disney animators. They include Squash and Stretch, Anticipation, Staging, Straight Ahead vs Pose-to-Pose, Follow Through and Overlapping Action, Slow In and Slow Out, Arcs, Secondary Action, Timing, Exaggeration, Solid Drawing, and Appeal. These principles help create believable movement and performance.

terms.title: Light Mapping
terms.summary: Light mapping is the process of baking lighting and shadow information into textures that are applied to static objects. It allows realistic lighting while keeping real-time performance costs low.

terms.title: LOD
terms.summary: Level of Detail (LOD) refers to multiple versions of an asset with decreasing complexity at different distances. This can include reduced geometry, simpler materials, or disabling lights to improve performance.

terms.title: Draw Calls
terms.summary: Draw calls are instructions sent from the CPU to the GPU to render objects. Each mesh, material slot, or actor increases draw calls. High draw call counts negatively impact performance, especially in Unreal Engine and indie projects where optimization is critical.

terms.title: Nanite
terms.summary: Nanite is Unreal Engine 5’s virtualized geometry system that allows extremely high-polygon models to render in real time by dynamically streaming only visible detail.

terms.title: Lumen
terms.summary: Lumen is Unreal Engine 5’s real-time global illumination system that simulates light bouncing and reflections dynamically without requiring baked lighting.

terms.title: Global Illumination
terms.summary: Global Illumination simulates how light bounces between surfaces, affecting color and brightness. Real-time solutions include Unreal’s Lumen, while offline renderers like Arnold and Cycles produce higher-quality but slower results.

terms.title: Bounce Light
terms.summary: Bounce light is indirect light that reflects off surfaces and illuminates other parts of a scene, contributing to realistic shading and color bleeding.

terms.title: 3-Point Lighting
terms.summary: Three-point lighting uses a key light, fill light, and back light to illuminate a subject clearly while maintaining depth and contrast.

terms.title: Key Light
terms.summary: The key light is the main light source in a scene, defining the overall lighting direction and strongest shadows.

terms.title: Fill Light
terms.summary: The fill light softens and reduces shadows created by the key light, helping control contrast.

terms.title: High Key vs Low Key
terms.summary: High-key lighting uses bright, even illumination with minimal shadows, while low-key lighting emphasizes contrast and deep shadows for dramatic effect.

terms.title: Exposure
terms.summary: Exposure determines how bright or dark an image appears based on light intensity and camera settings. In Unreal Engine, exposure can be controlled dynamically through post-process volumes.

terms.title: Post Process
terms.summary: Post-processing includes visual effects applied after rendering, such as color grading, bloom, depth of field, and exposure adjustments.

terms.title: Gestalt
terms.summary: Gestalt principles describe how humans perceive visual elements as unified wholes rather than separate pieces, influencing composition and design.

terms.title: Environment Artist
terms.summary:
An Environment Artist is a broad role in game development that can refer to two primary disciplines: Prop/Asset Art and Level Art. 

A Prop/Asset Artist focuses on creating high-quality individual assets. This often involves taking a blockout or proxy mesh and developing it into a finished prop using high-poly modeling (SubD or sculpting), retopology, baking, and PBR texturing. These artists may also create modular kits (like walls, doors, trims, and architectural pieces) designed to be reused across a level.

A Level Artist focuses on building and composing playable spaces inside the game engine. They take greybox/blockout levels and bring them to life using existing assets, creating mid-poly geometry when needed, applying trim sheets and tiling textures, set dressing, and establishing lighting and composition. Their work emphasizes visual storytelling, readability, performance, and guiding the player’s experience.

In production, both roles often overlap, but understanding the distinction helps artists specialize and work effectively within a game development pipeline.

terms.title: Gameplay Animator
terms.summary: A Gameplay Animator creates animations that respond to player input and gameplay systems, unlike cinematic animators who focus on pre-scripted scenes.

terms.title: JIRA
terms.summary: JIRA is a project management tool used in game development to track tasks, bugs, and production progress.

terms.title: Perforce
terms.summary: Perforce is a version control system widely used in game development for managing large files and team collaboration.

terms.title: Version Control
terms.summary: Version control systems track changes to files over time, allowing teams to collaborate and revert to previous versions. Examples include Git, Perforce, and SVN.

terms.title: Motivated vs Unmotivated Lighting
terms.summary: Motivated lighting comes from a believable source within the scene, like a lamp, window, or fire, helping the viewer understand where the light originates. Unmotivated lighting has no visible or logical source and is used stylistically to highlight subjects or improve readability. Strong lighting design often blends both approaches.

terms.title: Area / Rect Lights
terms.summary: Area (Rect) lights simulate large light sources and produce softer, more realistic shadows and reflections. In Unreal Engine 5, they are more expensive than point or directional lights because they calculate surface area, soft shadow falloff, and reflections, so overuse can negatively impact performance.

terms.title: PlayerStart Actor
terms.summary: The PlayerStart Actor defines where the player spawns when the level begins. It determines the player's starting position and orientation in the game world.

terms.title: Actor
terms.summary: An Actor is any object that exists in a level in Unreal Engine, including meshes, lights, cameras, and gameplay elements. Actors can contain components and logic that define their behavior.

terms.title: Control Rig
terms.summary: Control Rig allows animators to create rigs and animate characters directly inside Unreal Engine 5. It provides controls for posing, procedural animation, and editing without leaving the engine.

terms.title: Level Sequence
terms.summary: A Level Sequence is Unreal Engine’s cinematic timeline system used to animate cameras, actors, lights, and events over time. It works similarly to animation timelines in film or video editing software.

terms.title: Aperture
terms.summary: Aperture is the opening of a camera lens that controls how much light enters. A wider aperture (low f-stop) lets in more light and creates shallow depth of field, while a smaller aperture (high f-stop) results in a darker image with more of the scene in focus. Unreal’s cinematic cameras simulate this behavior.

terms.title: F-Stops
terms.summary: F-stops measure the size of a lens opening. Lower values (like f/1.8) mean more light and blurrier backgrounds, while higher values (like f/16) mean less light and sharper images. In Unreal Engine, f-stops affect both exposure and depth of field behavior.

terms.title: FOV vs Focal Length
terms.summary: Field of View (FOV) controls how wide the camera sees and is commonly used in gameplay cameras. Focal length controls lens behavior and is used in cinematic cameras. Wide FOV exaggerates perspective, while long focal lengths compress depth and feel more realistic.

terms.title: Focal Length
terms.summary: Focal length defines how a camera lens represents perspective. Short focal lengths (wide lenses) exaggerate space, while long focal lengths (telephoto lenses) compress depth. In Unreal and Maya, cinematic cameras rely on focal length instead of FOV for physically accurate results.

terms.title: Golden Ratio
terms.summary: The Golden Ratio (approximately 1.618) is a mathematical proportion used to create visually pleasing compositions. It is often visualized as a spiral guiding the viewer’s eye through an image.

terms.title: Phi Grid
terms.summary: The Phi Grid is based on the Golden Ratio and divides an image into sections that create more natural balance than the Rule of Thirds. It is used to place focal points more precisely.

terms.title: Rule of Thirds
terms.summary: The Rule of Thirds divides an image into a 3x3 grid. Placing important elements along the lines or intersections creates more engaging and balanced compositions.

terms.title: Principles of Design
terms.summary: The principles of design include balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, rhythm, unity, and variety. These concepts help organize visual elements to create clear, effective compositions.

terms.title: Line Quality
terms.summary: Line quality refers to the variation in thickness, darkness, and flow of lines. Strong line work uses variation to show depth, emphasize form, and guide the viewer’s eye.

terms.title: Edge Quality & Control
terms.summary: Edge quality describes how sharp or soft transitions are between forms. Artists use hard, soft, and lost edges to control focus. In sculpting, edge control defines form clarity and surface quality.

terms.title: Depth of Field
terms.summary: Depth of field determines how much of a scene is in focus. Shallow depth of field blurs the background to emphasize a subject. In Unreal Engine, this is controlled using aperture (low f-stop), focus distance, and cinematic camera or post-process settings.

terms.title: Monochromatic
terms.summary: A monochromatic color scheme uses variations of a single color, including tints (lighter), shades (darker), and tones (muted). This creates a cohesive and controlled look, often emphasizing value and form over color complexity.

terms.title: Complementary
terms.summary: Complementary colors are opposite each other on the color wheel (like blue and orange). When used together, they create strong contrast and visual energy, making subjects stand out.

terms.title: Analogous
terms.summary: Analogous colors sit next to each other on the color wheel (like blue, blue-green, and green). These schemes feel harmonious and natural because the colors are closely related.

terms.title: Analogous with Complementary Accent
terms.summary: This scheme uses an analogous palette for harmony but adds a small amount of a complementary color for contrast. This allows an image to feel unified while still having a strong focal point.

terms.title: Split Complementary
terms.summary: A split complementary scheme uses one base color and the two colors adjacent to its complement. It maintains strong contrast like complementary colors but is less intense and easier to balance.

terms.title: Color Wheel
terms.summary: The color wheel organizes colors and shows relationships like complementary and analogous schemes. In additive color (light, like screens), colors combine toward white (RGB). In subtractive color (paint/pigment), colors combine toward black or muddy tones (RYB/CMY). One important thing for artists to understand is that complementary colors are NOT always the same depending on which color system you are using. Traditional painting (RYB) uses pairs like red/green or blue/orange, while digital and lighting workflows (RGB) shift those relationships (PURPLE/green or blue/YELLOW). Because of this, what counts as a 'true complement' can change depending on whether you’re working in paint, Photoshop, or Unreal Engine, so always consider your medium.

terms.title: Color Temperature
terms.summary: Color temperature describes whether a color feels warm (reds, oranges) or cool (blues). In lighting, it is measured in Kelvin. Lower Kelvin values (like 2000K) produce warm light like fire, mid values (5000–6500K) resemble daylight, and higher values create cool, blue light. In Unreal and digital art, using Kelvin values can quickly achieve realistic lighting, such as warm campfires, glowing heated metal (which shifts from red to white as it heats), or neutral daylight.

terms.title: Inverse Square Law
terms.summary: The inverse square law states that light intensity decreases rapidly as distance increases. If you double the distance from a light, it becomes one-fourth as bright. Unreal Engine’s physically based lighting follows this rule, making correct light placement and scale critical for realism.

terms.title: Collision
terms.summary: Collision defines how objects physically interact in a game world. It determines where players can walk, what blocks movement, and how objects behave. Environment artists must create clean, optimized collision to ensure gameplay works correctly without hurting performance.

terms.title: Normals
terms.summary: Normals are vectors that tell a surface which direction it is facing, which is critical for how light interacts with that surface. Even simple geometry can appear smooth or faceted depending on how its normals are configured.

terms.title: Vertex Normals
terms.summary: Vertex normals define shading at each vertex and are averaged between faces to create smooth shading. When vertex normals are shared between faces, the surface appears smooth. When they are split, the surface appears hard or faceted. This is often referred to as soft vs hard edges.

terms.title: Face Normals
terms.summary: Face normals represent the direction of an individual polygon. When shading uses face normals instead of shared vertex normals, the object appears faceted, with visible polygon edges.

terms.title: Hard vs Soft Edges
terms.summary: Hard edges split vertex normals between faces, creating sharp transitions (faceted shading). Soft edges share vertex normals, smoothing the shading between faces. These do not change geometry—only how lighting is calculated.

terms.title: Face Weighted Normals
terms.summary: Face weighted normals adjust vertex normals so larger faces have more influence over shading. This helps hard surface models appear smoother and cleaner without adding extra geometry, making it especially useful in game art workflows.

terms.title: Smooth Shading vs Subdivision
terms.summary: A major point of confusion is that 'smoothing' can mean different things. In most 3D apps, smoothing refers to vertex normals being averaged to create smooth shading. In Maya, however, 'Smooth' often means subdividing geometry (adding more polygons). These are not the same—one changes shading, the other changes geometry.

terms.title: Texel Density
terms.summary: Texel density refers to how much texture resolution is applied across a surface. Consistent texel density ensures that all parts of an asset have similar visual sharpness, preventing some areas from looking blurry while others are overly detailed.

terms.title: World Aligned Texture
terms.summary: A world aligned texture applies a material based on world coordinates instead of UVs. This makes textures automatically align across multiple objects and is useful for environment work like terrain, cliffs, and large surfaces.

terms.title: Decals
terms.summary: Decals are projected textures used to add localized detail like dirt, damage, signs, or graffiti without modifying the base material. In Unreal, deferred decals allow detail layering while keeping assets modular and efficient.

terms.title: Shader Complexity
terms.summary: Shader complexity refers to how expensive a material is to render. More complex shaders require more GPU processing. Unreal Engine provides visualization modes to help artists identify and optimize costly materials.

terms.title: Lightmass vs Lumen
terms.summary: Lightmass is Unreal’s baked lighting system, where light is precomputed into lightmaps for performance. Lumen is Unreal Engine 5’s real-time global illumination system, dynamically calculating light bounces. Lightmass is more performance-friendly, while Lumen is more flexible and realistic in dynamic scenes.

terms.title: Root Motion
terms.summary: Root motion refers to animation where the character’s movement is driven by the animation itself (like walking forward). Instead of the game moving the character, the animation controls translation, which can increase realism but requires careful setup.

terms.title: In-Place Animation
terms.summary: In-place animation keeps the character moving in place (like running on a treadmill), while the game engine handles movement. This is common in games because it allows better control over speed and navigation.

terms.title: Animation Blueprint
terms.summary: An Animation Blueprint in Unreal Engine controls how animations play and blend based on gameplay logic. It allows developers to connect animations to player input, states, and transitions.

terms.title: State Machine
terms.summary: A state machine controls transitions between animations (such as idle, walk, run, jump). It defines rules for switching between states based on conditions like speed or player input.

terms.title: Blend Space
terms.summary: A blend space allows multiple animations to smoothly blend together based on input values like speed or direction. For example, blending between idle, walk, and run animations based on movement speed.

terms.title: Pivot / Origin
terms.summary: The pivot (or origin point) is the center point from which an object moves, rotates, and scales. Proper pivot placement is essential for animation, snapping objects together, and correct behavior in game engines.

terms.title: Scale
terms.summary: Scale refers to the size of objects in relation to real-world measurements. Maintaining correct scale is critical in Unreal Engine for physics, lighting, and player interaction to feel believable.

terms.title: Naming Conventions
terms.summary: Naming conventions are standardized ways of naming files, assets, and objects. Consistent naming helps teams stay organized, improves communication, and prevents errors in large projects.

terms.title: Optimization Budget
terms.summary: An optimization budget defines limits for things like triangle count, draw calls, and texture resolution. Artists must work within these limits to ensure the game runs smoothly while maintaining visual quality.

terms.title: Overdraw
terms.summary: Overdraw occurs when multiple transparent or layered pixels are rendered on top of each other, causing the GPU to repeatedly draw the same screen space. This commonly happens with foliage, particles, decals, and translucent materials. High overdraw is expensive because the GPU must process each layer even if it's hidden behind another. In Unreal Engine, overdraw is often visualized in debug views, and reducing it (by simplifying materials, limiting transparency, or adjusting mesh density) is critical for performance.

terms.title: Instruction Count
terms.summary: Instruction count refers to how many operations a shader performs to calculate the final pixel color. More instructions mean a more expensive material. Complex node setups, layered materials, and excessive math increase instruction count and reduce performance. In Unreal Engine’s Material Editor, instruction count is displayed to help artists optimize shaders and keep them within real-time performance budgets.

terms.title: Subdivision Modeling (SubD)
terms.summary: Subdivision Modeling (often called SubD) is a modeling technique where a relatively low poly count all quad mesh (called a Base Cage) is built with (usually) all quads and strong topology/edge loop flow, triple edges and/or creasing that is then subdivided to create a smoother, higher-resolution surface. This workflow is used in both film and video games. In feature film/VFX pipelines, SubD is often required because it allows for extremely high-resolution detail and 'infinite zoom' in close-up shots, as the model can be subdivided further whenever more detail is needed. In video games, SubD is commonly used for convenience—such as creating rounded shapes or preparing meshes for sculpting—but is not always required by the pipeline. SubD is also the foundation for sculpting workflows in programs like ZBrush, where artists work across multiple subdivision levels. A well-built Base Cage with clean topology and only the necessary edges is critical for achieving clean results when subdivided.

terms.title: Pipeline
terms.summary: A pipeline is the structured workflow that defines how assets are created, processed, and moved between departments in a production. In the entertainment industry, pipelines ensure that large teams can work efficiently and consistently. Pipelines differ depending on the industry: film/VFX pipelines prioritize high-quality offline rendering and often rely heavily on SubD and simulation workflows; animation pipelines focus on character rigging, animation, and storytelling; game development pipelines prioritize real-time performance, optimization, and engine integration (such as Unreal or Unity); and advertising pipelines often prioritize speed and flexibility to meet fast deadlines. Understanding the pipeline helps artists know what assets need to be created, how they should be built, and how they will be used later in production.

terms.title: Blueprint (BP)
terms.summary:
Blueprints (often abbreviated as BP) are Unreal Engine’s visual scripting system, allowing users to create logic, interactions, and behaviors without writing traditional code. Instead of typing code, users connect nodes in a graph to define how objects behave. 

In production, Blueprints are often named using the prefix "BP_" (for example: BP_Door, BP_LightSwitch), making it easy for teams to organize and identify interactive or logic-based assets within a project.

Blueprints are conceptually similar to prefabs in other engines like Unity. They act as reusable, self-contained assets that can include meshes, materials, collision, animations, and logic all in one place. Once created, a Blueprint can be reused multiple times throughout a level, and changes to it will update everywhere it is used.

For Environment Artists, Blueprints are an extremely powerful tool. While they are not required to be programmers, understanding Blueprints allows artists to add interactivity and polish to their work. Common use cases include setting up interactive doors, animated props, flickering lights, moving platforms, modular set pieces, or grouping multiple assets into a reusable kit. Blueprints can also control material parameters, lighting behaviors, and simple animations, helping environment artists create more dynamic and immersive scenes.

Learning Blueprints helps bridge the gap between art and gameplay, making artists more versatile and valuable within a game development pipeline.

terms.title: Static Mesh (SM)
terms.summary: A Static Mesh (often abbreviated as SM) is a 3D object in Unreal Engine that does not deform or animate (unlike skeletal meshes). These are the core building blocks of environments, including props, architecture, and set dressing elements. In production, Static Meshes are commonly named using the prefix "SM_" (for example: SM_Chair, SM_Wall_01), which helps organize projects and distinguish them from other asset types. Environment artists use Static Meshes extensively to populate levels, build modular kits, and construct worlds efficiently.

terms.title: Prefixes (Naming Conventions)
terms.summary: Prefixes are standardized naming conventions used in Unreal Engine to quickly identify the type of asset. They help teams stay organized and prevent confusion in large projects. Common examples include: SM_ (Static Mesh), BP_ (Blueprint), MI_ (Material Instance), M_ (Material), T_ (Texture), SK_ (Skeletal Mesh), and NI_ or NS_ (Niagara Systems). Using consistent prefixes improves workflow, asset management, and collaboration across teams.

terms.title: Scripting
terms.summary:
Scripting refers to creating logic and behavior in a game using systems like Unreal Engine’s Blueprints (visual scripting) or code-based systems. Blueprints allow users to connect nodes to define interactions, events, and gameplay behaviors without writing traditional code.

There are two primary Blueprint contexts: regular Blueprint Actors (reusable assets placed in the world) and Level Blueprints. Level Blueprints are tied to a specific level and are often used for one-off scripted events such as opening a door when the player enters an area, triggering a cinematic, or coordinating lighting and effects.

Environment artists can use scripting to add interactivity and storytelling to their scenes—for example, triggering lights to flicker, animating environmental props, or creating a scripted moment where something happens when the player reaches a certain point. Understanding basic scripting helps artists bring their environments to life and collaborate more effectively with designers and programmers.

terms.title: Technical Artist
terms.summary:
A Technical Artist is a hybrid role that bridges the gap between art and programming in game development. The exact responsibilities can vary significantly between studios, but generally fall into a few key areas.

Some Technical Artists focus on advanced look development, creating complex shaders, materials, and rendering solutions that push visual quality. Others focus on building tools and pipelines, using systems like Unreal Editor Utility Widgets, Blueprints, or Python to streamline workflows and improve efficiency for artists. Another major area is optimization, where Technical Artists analyze performance (such as draw calls, shader cost, and memory usage) and help ensure the game runs efficiently.

Because the role varies so much, Technical Artists must be adaptable problem solvers who understand both artistic goals and technical constraints. They often act as a bridge between departments, helping artists achieve high-quality visuals while staying within performance and engine limitations.

terms.title: Keyframes
terms.summary:
Keyframes are specific points in time where a value (such as position, rotation, scale, or any animated property) is defined. Animation systems then interpolate between these keyframes to create motion over time.

In both Maya and Unreal Engine, different types of interpolation between keyframes control how motion behaves:

- Linear interpolation moves at a constant speed between keyframes. This is useful for maintaining consistent motion, such as camera fly-throughs where you want steady movement between cuts.

- Cubic (Bezier) interpolation is the most commonly used type and allows for smooth transitions. It creates ease-in and ease-out motion (also called "slow in/slow out"), where movement gradually accelerates and decelerates. This is essential for natural and believable animation.

- Stepped interpolation holds a value until the next keyframe without blending. This is often used for blocking animation, previewing poses, or creating sudden changes.

In Maya, these interpolation types are controlled through the Graph Editor using animation curves. In Unreal Engine, they are used in Sequencer and Animation Blueprints, allowing artists to control timing and motion directly in-engine.

For artists, understanding keyframe interpolation is critical because it determines not just where something moves, but how it moves. Choosing the right interpolation type can make the difference between animation that feels robotic versus smooth, intentional, and cinematic.

terms.title: Skeleton (Bones & Joints vs Control Rig)
terms.summary:
A skeleton in animation is a hierarchical system of bones and joints used to deform and animate a character or object. The skeleton defines how different parts of a model are connected and how they move relative to each other.

Bones are the structural segments (like arms, legs, spine), while joints are the connection points where movement occurs (like elbows or knees). Together, they form the underlying structure that drives deformation when a character moves.

A helpful way to think about this is like a puppet:
- The skeleton (bones and joints) is like the internal structure or hinges that define how the puppet can bend and move.
- The Control Rig is like the external controls (strings or control bars) that the animator uses to actually manipulate the puppet.

Control rigs do NOT deform the mesh directly—instead, they control the skeleton, which then drives the deformation of the model. This makes animation easier and more intuitive, allowing animators to use handles and controls rather than rotating individual bones manually.

In production, the skeleton is built for structure and deformation, while the control rig is designed for usability and animation performance. Understanding the difference helps artists work more effectively in both rigging and animation workflows.

terms.title: Rigging
terms.summary: Rigging is the process of building a system that allows a 3D model to be animated. This includes creating a skeleton (bones and joints), setting up controls (Control Rig), and preparing the model so it moves in a believable and usable way. A good rig provides intuitive controls for animators while maintaining proper deformation and performance.

terms.title: Skinning
terms.summary: Skinning is the process of attaching (binding) a 3D mesh to a skeleton so that it moves when the bones are animated. Each vertex of the mesh is influenced by one or more bones, allowing the model to deform as the skeleton moves.

terms.title: Weight Painting
terms.summary: Weight painting controls how much influence each bone has over parts of a mesh. Artists paint values onto the model to define how it deforms when animated. Clean weight painting ensures smooth bending at joints like elbows and knees without unnatural stretching or collapsing.

terms.title: Cycles (Animation)
terms.summary: An animation cycle is a repeating sequence of motion, such as a walk cycle, run cycle, or idle loop. Cycles are commonly used in games to create continuous motion efficiently without needing unique animation for every step.

terms.title: Move Set
terms.summary: A move set is the collection of animations a character can perform in a game, such as walking, running, jumping, attacking, or idling. Designing a complete move set ensures a character can respond to all gameplay situations.

terms.title: Layered Animation Technique
terms.summary: Layered animation builds motion in multiple passes instead of all at once. Animators block major movement first, then refine details like secondary motion and overlap. This approach helps manage complexity and improve results.

terms.title: Straight Ahead Animation
terms.summary: Straight Ahead animation is created frame-by-frame in sequence, without planning key poses first. It encourages fluid, organic motion but can be harder to control and revise.

terms.title: Pose to Pose Animation
terms.summary: Pose to Pose animation begins by defining key poses first, then filling in the motion between them. This approach provides better planning, structure, and control over timing and storytelling.

terms.title: Stepped Key Animation
terms.summary: Stepped key animation uses stepped interpolation so there is no in-between motion between keyframes. This is often used during blocking to quickly evaluate poses and timing without smoothing.

terms.title: Curve Editor
terms.summary: The Curve Editor is a tool used to visualize and edit animation curves over time. In Maya (Graph Editor) and Unreal Engine (Sequencer), it allows animators to control interpolation, timing, and easing between keyframes. Adjusting curves is critical for refining motion, controlling speed changes, and achieving natural movement.

terms.title: Metallic Map
terms.summary:
A metallic map determines whether a material behaves like a metal or a non-metal in a PBR workflow. Metallic values affect how light reflects from the surface, how reflections are colored, and how the material interacts with its Base Color. In most game art pipelines, metallic maps are typically binary: 0 (black) for non-metals such as wood, plastic, fabric, rubber, and stone, and 1 (white) for metals such as steel, aluminum, gold, and copper.

Unlike Roughness maps, metallic maps usually contain very little grayscale variation. Most surfaces are either metal or non-metal. Grayscale values are typically reserved for areas where different materials meet, such as chipped paint revealing bare metal underneath.

Key takeaway: Use black for non-metals and white for metals whenever possible. Let the Roughness map create most of the surface variation and realism, while the Metallic map simply defines how the material fundamentally responds to light.

terms.title: Normal Map
terms.summary:
A normal map is a texture that simulates small surface details by altering how light interacts with a model without adding extra geometry. It creates the illusion of depth, bumps, grooves, wrinkles, and surface texture while keeping the mesh relatively low in polygon count. This allows game artists to achieve high-detail visuals while maintaining performance.

Normal maps are commonly generated by baking detail from a high-resolution model onto a lower-resolution game asset. Details such as panel lines, bolts, fabric weave, cracks, and sculpted surface features can all be represented through a normal map.

Unlike a Roughness map, a Normal map does not control reflections or material properties. Instead, it changes the direction a surface appears to face, affecting how light and shadows react across the model.

Key takeaway: Normal maps add the illusion of geometric detail, while Roughness maps control how light behaves on the surface. A strong material often relies on both working together to create believable realism.

terms.title: PBR Workflow
terms.summary: Physically Based Rendering (PBR) is a material workflow used in modern game engines such as Unreal Engine and Unity. PBR materials follow real-world lighting principles so assets react consistently under different lighting conditions. The most common workflow uses Base Color, Roughness, Metallic, and Normal maps.

terms.title: Spline
terms.summary: A spline is a smooth curve defined by points that can be used in multiple ways across disciplines. In animation, splines define motion through curves and trajectories. In modeling and level design, splines can be used to create paths, roads, fences, or cables. In Unreal Engine, spline-based Blueprints are often used to generate modular assets like fences or roads procedurally along a path.

terms.title: SDF (Signed Distance Fields)
terms.summary: Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) represent the distance between a point in space and the nearest surface. In Unreal Engine, they are used for features like distance field shadows, ambient occlusion, and effects like soft intersections. They enable efficient lighting and effects calculations in real time.

terms.title: Motion Matching
terms.summary: Motion Matching is an advanced animation system that selects the best animation frame from a large database based on player input and movement context. Instead of blending between predefined states, it dynamically chooses the most appropriate motion, creating highly responsive and realistic movement.

terms.title: Starts and Stops
terms.summary:
Starts and Stops describe how motion begins and ends, emphasizing acceleration (ease-in) and deceleration (ease-out). Strong animation avoids sudden motion changes and instead gradually builds and reduces energy, making movement feel grounded and believable.

In game development, this concept goes beyond a single animation clip. Animators often break motion into separate pieces—such as start, loop, and stop animations (for example: walk_start, walk_loop, walk_stop). These pieces are exported individually and then combined in Unreal Engine using an Animation Blueprint (AnimBP).

In a traditional State Machine workflow, these animations are connected through transitions (idle → start → loop → stop → idle), allowing the game to switch between them based on player input and conditions.

In a Motion Matching workflow, instead of manually defining transitions, the system dynamically selects the most appropriate frame from a large animation dataset based on movement input, automatically handling starts and stops more fluidly.

Understanding how to break motion into modular parts and how those parts are used in-engine is critical for creating responsive, believable gameplay animation.

terms.title: Pre & Post Infinity (Cycle Controls)
terms.summary:
Pre and Post Infinity (often called Out-of-Range behavior in Unreal or Curve Infinity settings in Maya’s Graph Editor) control how animation behaves before the first keyframe and after the last keyframe.

Common behaviors include:
- Cycle (Repeat): The animation loops continuously.
- Ping Pong (Oscillate): The animation plays forward, then backward repeatedly.
- Offset / Relative Cycle: The animation repeats while continuing to add movement or offset each cycle (useful for things like looping motion that travels forward).
- Constant: Holds the value of the first or last keyframe.

In Maya, these are referred to as Pre Infinity and Post Infinity settings in the Graph Editor. In Unreal Engine, similar behavior can be achieved through Sequencer or animation looping settings.

These tools are essential for extending animations without adding extra keyframes, especially for loops like walk cycles, environmental motion, or repeated mechanical actions.

terms.title: 180 Degree Rule
terms.summary: The 180 Degree Rule is a guideline that keeps the camera on one side of an imaginary line between subjects. This maintains consistent screen direction and spatial relationships. Breaking this rule can confuse the viewer because characters or objects can appear to flip positions on screen.

terms.title: Dolly
terms.summary: A dolly shot moves the entire camera physically forward or backward through space. This creates a sense of depth and immersion, as objects shift in perspective relative to the camera.

terms.title: Pan
terms.summary: A pan rotates the camera left or right on its vertical axis without moving its position. It is often used to follow subjects or reveal parts of a scene.

terms.title: Pedestal (Tilt Up/Down)
terms.summary: A pedestal shot moves the camera vertically up or down without tilting it. This differs from a tilt, which rotates the camera while staying in place. Pedestal movement physically raises or lowers the camera’s position.

terms.title: Truck
terms.summary: A truck shot moves the camera side-to-side (left or right) through space. It is useful for following characters or creating parallax to enhance depth.

terms.title: Zoom
terms.summary: A zoom changes the focal length of the lens, making the subject appear closer or farther away without moving the camera. Unlike a dolly, a zoom does not change perspective or parallax.

terms.title: Dolly Zoom (Zolly)
terms.summary: A dolly zoom (or zolly) combines moving the camera forward or backward while simultaneously adjusting the zoom. This creates a dramatic effect where the subject stays the same size while the background appears to stretch or compress.

terms.title: Crane Shot
terms.summary: A crane shot moves the camera through space vertically and often horizontally using a boom or crane-like motion. It is used to create sweeping, cinematic movements and reveal large environments.

terms.title: Full Shot
terms.summary: A full shot frames a subject’s entire body from head to toe. It is often used to show character movement, silhouette, and interaction with the environment.

terms.title: Two Shot
terms.summary: A two shot frames two characters within the same composition. It is commonly used to show interaction, relationships, or dialogue between subjects.

terms.title: Dutch Angle
terms.summary: A Dutch angle tilts the camera so the horizon line is no longer level. This creates a sense of tension, unease, or disorientation in the viewer.

terms.title: Match Cut
terms.summary: A match cut transitions between two shots by matching composition, shape, or motion. This creates a smooth visual connection between scenes and can emphasize thematic or narrative continuity.

terms.title: Jump Cut
terms.summary: A jump cut is an abrupt transition between two similar shots that creates a noticeable 'jump' in time or position. While sometimes used stylistically, it is often considered a mistake in portfolios because it can feel unpolished or unintentional and disrupt visual continuity.
